author.name: Apollodorus
author.lead: A certain "Apollodorus" is indicated as author on some surviving manuscripts, this Apollodorus has been mistakenly identified with Apollodorus of Athens (born c. 180 BCE), a student of Aristarchus of Samothrace who also worked in Alexandria. It is known—from references in the minor scholia on Homer—that Apollodorus of Athens did leave a similar comprehensive repertory on mythology, in the form of a verse chronicle. The mistaken attribution was made by scholars following mention of the name by Photius I of Constantinople, though Photius did not name him as the Athenian and the name was in common use at the time. For chronological reasons, Apollodorus of Athens could not have written the book, the author of the Bibliotheca is at times referred to as the "Pseudo-Apollodorus", to distinguish him from Apollodorus of Athens. Modern works often simply call him "Apollodorus". The work is generally dated to the first or second centuries AD.

Bibliotheca (Apollodorus).title: Bibliotheca (Apollodorus)
Bibliotheca (Apollodorus).lead: The Bibliotheca is a compendium of Greek myths and heroic legends, genealogical tables and histories arranged in three books, generally dated to the first or second century AD. The work is commonly described as having been written by Apollodorus (or sometimes Pseudo-Apollodorus), a result of its false attribution to the 2nd-century BC scholar Apollodorus of Athens.

primary.heading: Manuscript tradition
primary.text: The first mention of the work is by Photius, patriarch of Constantinople in 9th century CE, in his "account of books read". The last section of the Bibliotheca, which breaks off during the section on Theseus, is missing in surviving manuscripts. However, Photius had the full work and mentions that the lost section had myths about the heroes of the Trojan War. Byzantine author John Tzetes, who lived in Constantinople in the twelfth century, often cited the Bibliotheca in his writings. The Bibliotheca was almost lost in the 13th century, surviving in one now-incomplete manuscript, which was copied for Cardinal Bessarion in the 15th century. Any surviving manuscripts of the Bibliotheca are descended from a fourteenth-century manuscript in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, in Paris.

secondary.heading: Scholarship
secondary.text: The Bibliotheca has been referenced in scholarship throughout history. As a mythographical work it has influenced scholarship on Greek mythology. An epigram recorded by the important intellectual Patriarch Photius I of Constantinople expressed its purpose: It has the following not ungraceful epigram: "Draw your knowledge of the past from me and read the ancient tales of learned lore. Look neither at the page of Homer, nor of elegy, nor tragic muse, nor epic strain. Seek not the vaunted verse of the cycle; but look in me and you will find in me all that the world contains". Photius is one of the first surviving reviews of the use of the Bibliotheca in the field. Throughout the 12th and 13th centuries CE, the Bibliotheca was referred to in scholarship about Ancient Greece most often found in letters from scholars of the time.

Q102561.label: Sisyphus
Q102561.description: king of Ephyra in Greek mythology
Q102561.lead: In Greek mythology, Sisyphus or Sisyphos is the founder and king of Ephyra (now known as Corinth). He reveals Zeus's abduction of Aegina to the river god Asopus, thereby incurring Zeus's wrath.

Q102884.label: Mnemosyne
Q102884.description: personification of memory in Greek mythology, mother of the nine muses
Q102884.lead: In Greek mythology, Mnemosyne was one of the Titans, who are the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the goddess of memory and the mother of the nine Muses by Zeus.

Q103107.label: Leto
Q103107.description: Greek mythological figure and mother of Apollo and Artemis
Q103107.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Leto is the mother of Apollo and Artemis. She is the daughter of the Titans Coeus and Phoebe, and the sister of Asteria.

Q10350754.label: Poeas
Q10350754.description: Argonaut and friend of Heracles in Greek mythology
Q10350754.lead: In Greek mythology, Poeas, or Poias was a king of Meliboea or Malis (Maleae) and one of the Argonauts.

Q103968.label: Clio
Q103968.description: Greek mythological person, muse of history or of lyre playing, daughter of Zeus and the Titaness Mnemosyne
Q103968.lead: In Greek mythology, Clio, also spelled Kleio, Cleio, or Cleo, is the muse of history, or in a few mythological accounts, the muse of lyre-playing.

Q103975.label: Calliope
Q103975.lead: In Greek mythology, Calliope is the Muse who presides over eloquence and epic poetry, so called from the ecstatic harmony of her voice. Hesiod and Ovid called her the "Chief of all Muses".

Q103992.label: Melpomene
Q103992.lead: Melpomene is the Muse of tragedy in Greek mythology. She is described as the daughter of Zeus and Mnemosyne (and therefore of power and memory) along with the other Muses, and she is often portrayed with a tragic theatrical mask.

Q104012.label: Euterpe
Q104012.description: muse of music in Greek mythology
Q104012.lead: Euterpe was one of the Muses in Greek mythology, presiding over music. In late Classical times, she was named muse of lyric poetry.

Q1043413.label: Chrysippus
Q1043413.lead: In Greek mythology, Chrysippus was a divine hero of Elis in the Peloponnesus peninsula (southern Greece), sometimes referred to as Chrysippus of Pisa. He is traditionally the son of Pelops by a nymph, born out of wedlock.

Q1045730.label: Thersites
Q1045730.description: son of Agrius, Achean warrior in the Trojan War
Q1045730.lead: In Greek mythology, Thersites was a soldier of the Greek army during the Trojan War.

Q1045732.label: Mimas
Q1045732.lead: In Greek mythology, Mimas was one of the Gigantes (Giants), the offspring of Gaia, born from the blood of the castrated Uranus.

Q1052877.label: Stheno
Q1052877.description: monster from Greek mythology, eldest of the Gorgons
Q1052877.lead: In Greek mythology, Stheno and Euryale ( yuu-RY-ə-lee; Ancient Greek: Εὐρυάλη, romanized: Euryálē, lit. 'far-roaming') were two of the three sister Gorgons, the third being Medusa, who were able to turn anyone who looked at them to stone. Unlike the mortal Medusa, both Stheno and Euryale were immortal.

Q10546716.label: Cnossia
Q10546716.description: misstress of Menelaus in Greek myth
Q10546716.lead: Cnossia was a nymph or slave in Greek mythology. By Menelaus, king of Sparta, she mothered a son named Xenodamus.

Q105773029.label: Pieris
Q105773029.lead: In Greek mythology, Pieris was one of the names given for the slave who was the mother, by Menelaus, of Megapenthes. Homer's Odyssey, and the geographer Pausanias, mention that Megapenthes was the illegitimate son of Menelaus, king of Mycenaean Sparta, by a slave, without naming her.

Q1061554.label: Polydorus
Q1061554.description: mythological Theban prince, son of Cadmus
Q1061554.lead: In Greek mythology, Polydorus or Polydoros was a king of Thebes.

Q1061782.label: Rhesus of Thrace
Q1061782.lead: Rhesus is a mythical king of Thrace in The Iliad who fought on the side of Trojans. Rhesus arrived late to the battle and, while he slept in his camp after arriving, Diomedes and Odysseus killed him and stole his team of horses during a night raid.

Q1062299.label: Sthenelus
Q1062299.lead: In Greek mythology, Sthenelus was a king of Tiryns and Mycenae, and the son of Perseus who founded the latter city.

Q106448330.label: Polygonus
Q106448330.lead: In Greek mythology, Polygonus was the Thracian son of the sea god Proteus by Torone, the daughter of Cleitus. He was the brother of Telegonus.

Q1065774.label: Lacedaemon
Q1065774.lead: Lacedaemon or Lacaedemon was the eponymous king of Lacedaemon (i.e. Sparta) in classical Greek mythology.

Q1072573.label: Niobe
Q1072573.lead: In Greek mythology, Niobe was a daughter of Phoroneus and Teledice, the sister of Apis, and the mother by Zeus of Argus, who was the eponym of Argos. She may have appeared in the lost genealogical epic Catalogue of Women, as part of the family tree of Inachids, one of the mythological royal dynasties of Argos.

Q107785.label: Amalthea
Q107785.lead: In Greek mythology, Amalthea or Amaltheia is the figure most commonly identified as the nurse of Zeus during his infancy. She is described either as a nymph who raises the child on the milk of a goat or, in some accounts from the Hellenistic period (c. 323–30 BC) onwards, as the goat itself.

Q108019.label: Thalia
Q108019.description: Muse of comedy in Greek mythology
Q108019.lead: In Greek mythology, Thalia, also spelled Thaleia, was one of the Muses, the goddess who presided over comedy and idyllic poetry. In this context her name means "flourishing", because the praises in her songs flourish through time.

Q108419.label: Rhea
Q108419.description: female Titan in Greek mythology, mother of Zeus and mother of Hera
Q108419.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhea, Rhia or Rheia was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the sister and wife of Cronus, and by him was the mother of Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Zeus.

Q108541872.label: Mnesileus
Q108541872.lead: In Greek mythology, Mnesileus or Mnasinous (Μνασίνους) was the son of Polydeuces, one of the Dioscuri, and Phoebe, daughter of Leucippus of Messenia. The temple of the Dioscuri at Argos contained also the statues of these two sons of the Dioscuri, Anaxias and Mnasinous, and on the throne of Amyclae both were represented riding on horseback.

Q1088990.label: Chthonius
Q1088990.description: Greek mythical character, one of the Spartoi

Q109220.label: Boreas
Q109220.description: Greek mythological personification and god of the North wind, storms,, winter, loneliness, solitude, absence, lack, sadness, depression, calmness and serenity
Q109220.lead: Boreas is the Greek god of the cold north wind, storms, and winter. Although he was normally taken as the north wind, the Roman writers Aulus Gellius and Pliny the Elder both took Boreas as a northeast wind, equivalent to the Roman god Aquilo or Septentrio.

Q109236480.label: Hyleus
Q109236480.description: mythological hunter killed by Calydonian boar
Q109236480.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyleus was one of heroes who participated in the Calydonian boar hunt. While the hunters surrounded the brute and slew it, Hyleus as well as Ancaeus were unlucky, as they were both killed by it.

Q10966726.label: Aegialeus
Q10966726.description: King of Argos, son of Adrastus
Q10966726.lead: Aegialeus also Aegealeus, Aigialeus, Egialeus, was the elder son of Adrastus, a king of Argos, and either Amphithea or Demonassa.

Q112001.label: Taygete
Q112001.description: one of the Pleiades in Greek mythology
Q112001.lead: In Classical Greek mythology, Taygete was a nymph, one of the Pleiades according to the Bibliotheca (3.10.1) and a companion of Artemis, in her archaic role as potnia theron, "Mistress of the animals", with its likely roots in prehistory. Mount Taygetos in Laconia, dedicated to the goddess, was her haunt.

Q1125040.label: Eriphyle
Q1125040.description: daughter of Talaus in Greek mythology
Q1125040.lead: Eriphyle was a figure in Greek mythology who, in exchange for the Necklace of Harmonia (also called the Necklace of Eriphyle) given to her by Polynices, persuaded her husband Amphiaraus to join the doomed expedition of the Seven against Thebes. She was then slain by her son Alcmaeon.

Q1125049.label: Eumolpus
Q1125049.description: Thracian king settled at Eleusis in Greek mythology
Q1125049.lead: In Greek Mythology, Eumolpus was a legendary king of Thrace. He was described as having come to Attica either as a bard, a warrior, or a priest of Demeter and Dionysus.

Q1126715.label: Tyro
Q1126715.description: daughter of Salmoneus in Greek mythology
Q1126715.lead: In Greek mythology, Tyro was an Elean princess who later became Queen of Iolcus.

Q1128881.label: Eurytion
Q1128881.description: king of Phthia in Greek mythology
Q1128881.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurytion or Eurythion (Ancient Greek: Εὐρυθίων) was a king of Phthia. He was also counted among the Argonauts and the Calydonian hunters.

Q1128942.label: Parthenopeus
Q1128942.description: son of Melanion in Greek mythology
Q1128942.lead: In Greek mythology, Parthenopaeus or Parthenopaios was one of the Seven against Thebes, a native of Arcadia, described as young and outstandingly good-looking, but at the same time arrogant, ruthless and over-confident, although an unproblematic ally for the Argives.

Q11291639.label: Oeax
Q11291639.description: son of Nauplius in Greek mythology
Q11291639.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Oeax was a Euboean prince as the son of King Nauplius.

Q11294144.label: Castor
Q11294144.description: Greek mythical figure, brother of Pollux

Q1129489.label: Orithyia
Q1129489.lead: In Greek mythology, Orithyia or Oreithyia was an Athenian princess who was raped by Boreas, the north wind, and gave birth to the twin Boreads, Zetes and Calaïs.

Q1129914.label: Libya
Q1129914.description: goddess in Roman and Greek mythology
Q1129914.lead: Libya, Libye, Lybie or Lybee was the daughter of Epaphus, King of Egypt, in both Greek and Roman mythology. She personified the land of Ancient Libya in North Africa, and was considered by the Greeks to be the origin of the name of what is now Libya.

Q1131643.label: Salmoneus
Q1131643.description: son of Aiolos in Greek mythology
Q1131643.lead: In Greek mythology, Salmoneus was 'the wicked' eponymous king and founder of Salmone in Pisatis.

Q1135152.label: Pholus
Q1135152.lead: In Greek mythology, Pholus was a wise centaur and friend of Heracles who lived in a cave on or near Mount Pelion.

Q1136130.label: Idas
Q1136130.description: son of Aphareus, husband of Marpessa, argonaut in Greek mythology
Q1136130.lead: In Greek mythology, Idas, was a Messenian prince. He was one of the Argonauts, a participant in the hunt for the Calydonian Boar, and contender with the gods.

Q1138506.label: Tereus
Q1138506.lead: In Greek mythology, Tereus was a Thracian king, the son of Ares and the naiad Bistonis. He was the brother of Dryas.

Q1139448.label: Dorus
Q1139448.description: son of Hellen, eponym of the Dorians in Greek mythology
Q1139448.lead: In Greek mythology, Dorus was the eponymous founder of the Dorians.

Q1139470.label: Procris
Q1139470.lead: In Greek mythology, Procris was an Athenian princess, the third daughter of Erechtheus, king of Athens and his wife, Praxithea. Homer mentions her in the Odyssey as one of the many dead spirits Odysseus saw in the Underworld.

Q1141300.label: Celeus
Q1141300.lead: Celeus or Keleos (pronounced /ke.le.ós/, keh-leh-OSS; ) was the king of Eleusis in Greek mythology, husband of Metaneira and father of several daughters, who are called Callidice, Demo, Cleisidice and Callithoe in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, and Diogeneia, Pammerope and Saesara by Pausanias.

Q1145956.label: Phoenix
Q1145956.description: Greek mythological character, son of Agenor and Telephassa, eponym of Phoenicia
Q1145956.lead: In Greek mythology, Phoenix or Phoinix was the eponym of Phoenicia who together with his brothers were tasked to find their abducted sister Europa.

Q1154304.label: Nicostratus
Q1154304.description: son of Menelaus and Helen of Troy
Q1154304.lead: In Greek mythology, Nicostratus is a son of Menelaus, the king of Sparta. He was known to Hesiod and epic poet Cinaethon.

Q115449.label: Philomela
Q115449.description: legendary princess of Athens transformed into a swallow or nightingale
Q115449.lead: Philomela or Philomel is a minor figure in Greek mythology who is frequently invoked as a direct and figurative symbol in literary and artistic works in the Western canon.

Q1164796.label: Procles
Q1164796.description: Procles son of Aristodemus, Spartan king
Q1164796.lead: In Greek legends, Procles was one of the Heracleidae, a great-great-great-grandson of Heracles, and a son of Aristodemus and Argia. His twin was Eurysthenes.

Q116642.label: Polydora
Q116642.description: daughter of Peleus in Greek mythology

Q1172040.label: Amyntor
Q1172040.description: son of Ormenos and father of Phoenix
Q1172040.lead: In Greek mythology, Amyntor was the son of Ormenus, and a king of Eleon or Ormenium. Amyntor's son Phoenix, on his mother's urgings, had sex with his father's concubine, Clytia or Phthia.

Q1178970.label: Porthaon
Q1178970.description: son of Agenor in Greek mythology
Q1178970.lead: In Greek mythology, Porthaon, sometimes referred to as Parthaon or Portheus, was a king of Calydon and son of Agenor or Ares by Epicaste and thus brother of Demonice (also known as Demodice) and possibly Thestius.

Q1186488.label: Demonice
Q1186488.lead: In Greek mythology, Demonice was a Aetolian princess as the daughter of King Agenor of Pleuron and Epicaste and thus sister of Porthaon and in some account, Thestius. She bore Ares four sons: Evenus, Molus, Pylus, and Thestius.

Q1187298.label: Gyges
Q1187298.description: one of the Hundred-Handers, or hekatonkheires

Q11921121.label: Aethra
Q11921121.lead: In Greek mythology, Aethra or Aithra was a Troezenian princess and the daughter of King Pittheus.

Q12046224.label: Pollux
Q12046224.description: Greek mythical figure, brother of Castor

Q1206572.label: Podarces
Q1206572.lead: In Greek mythology, Podarces was a son of Iphiclus (son of Phylacus, founder of Phylace) by Diomedeia and the brother of Protesilaus. In some accounts, he and his brother were called the sons of Phylacus and Astyoche instead.

Q122248.label: Heracles
Q122248.description: divine hero in Greek mythology, son of Zeus and Alcmene
Q122248.lead: Heracles, born Alcaeus (Ἀλκαῖος) or Alcides (Ἀλκείδης), was the greatest of the Greek heroes. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and the foster son of Amphitryon.

Q122783241.label: Phthia
Q122783241.description: mythological Greek character, lover of Amyntor
Q122783241.lead: In Greek mythology, Phthia or Clytia (Ancient Greek: Κλυτία, romanized: Klutía, lit. 'renowned') is the concubine of Amyntor, king of Ormenium. She became the reason for the falling out between Amyntor and his son Phoenix after Phoenix slept with her.

Q1230535.label: Thoas
Q1230535.description: father of Hypsipyle in ancient Greek mythology, son of Dionysus
Q1230535.lead: In Greek mythology, Thoas was a son of the god Dionysus and Ariadne, the daughter of the Cretan king Minos. He was the king of Lemnos when the Lemnian women decided to kill all the men on the island.

Q1231743.label: Procne
Q1231743.description: legendary princess of Athens, sister of Philomele
Q1231743.lead: Procne or Progne is a minor figure in Greek and Roman mythology. Traditionally she is an Athenian princess as the elder daughter of a king of Athens named Pandion.

Q1232714.label: Glaucus
Q1232714.description: son of Sisyphus, mythical Corinthian king
Q1232714.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Glaucus, usually surnamed as Potnieus, was a son of Sisyphus whose main myth involved his violent death as the result of his horsemanship. He was the king of the Boeotian city of Potniae or sometimes of Corinth.

Q1233841.label: Polybotes
Q1233841.description: one of the Giants of Greek mythology
Q1233841.lead: In Greek mythology, Polybotes was one of the giants, the offspring of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). He fought Poseidon during the Gigantomachy, the war between the giants and the gods.

Q1237258.label: Metope
Q1237258.lead: In Greek mythology, Metope may refer to the following: Metope, the Arcadian naiad daughter of the river god Ladon, thus sister to Daphne. Her waters were near the town of Stymphalus in the Peloponnesus.

Q1237732.label: Toxeus
Q1237732.description: mythological Greek character, son of Oineus

Q1249335.label: Gelanor
Q1249335.description: mythical son of Sthenelas of Argos
Q1249335.lead: In Greek mythology, Pelasgus also known as Gelanor, was an Inachid king of Argos.

Q1250023.label: Maera
Q1250023.description: mythical dog of Icarius of Attica
Q1250023.lead: In Greek mythology, Maera is the hound of Erigone, daughter of Icarius of Athens.

Q1258941.label: Illyrius
Q1258941.description: son of Polyphemus in Greek mythology
Q1258941.lead: Illyrius is the son of Cadmus and Harmonia, who eventually ruled Illyria and became the eponymous ancestor of the Illyrians. Illyrius/Illyriós/Illyri is a name known in different stories found in ancient Greek mythology.

Q12626619.label: Acheron
Q12626619.description: god of river of underworld, Greek mythology

Q1280725.label: Echion
Q1280725.description: one of the Spartoi, father of Pentheus

Q128176.label: Agamemnon
Q128176.description: son of Atreus in Greek mythology
Q128176.lead: In Greek mythology, Agamemnon was a king of Mycenae who commanded the Achaeans during the Trojan War. He was the son (or grandson) of King Atreus and Queen Aerope, the brother of Menelaus, the husband of Clytemnestra, and the father of Iphigenia, Iphianassa, Electra, Laodike, Orestes and Chrysothemis.

Q128430.label: cyclops
Q128430.description: member of a primordial race of giants in Greek mythology and later Roman mythology
Q128430.lead: In Greek mythology and later Roman mythology, the Cyclopes are giant one-eyed creatures. Three kinds of Cyclopes can be distinguished.

Q1289213.label: Thersander
Q1289213.lead: In Greek mythology, the name Thersander or Thersandros was one of the Epigoni, who attacked the city of Thebes. This is in retaliation for the deaths of their fathers, the war of the Seven against Thebes, who had attempted the same thing.

Q1292797.label: Sidero
Q1292797.lead: In Greek mythology, Sidero was the second wife of King Salmoneus of Elis and stepmother of Tyro, whom she mistreated. Pelias and Neleus, Tyro's twin sons, sought revenge when they reached adulthood.

Q1294873.label: Erginus
Q1294873.lead: In Greek mythology, Erginus was a king of Minyan Orchomenus in Boeotia.

Q1294888.label: Ascalaphus
Q1294888.description: mythological Greek character, deity of the underground
Q1294888.lead: In Greek mythology, Ascalaphus was the son of Acheron and Orphne.

Q12958119.label: Latona
Q12958119.description: mother of Apollo and Diana in Roman mythology

Q129866.label: Minotaur
Q129866.description: creature of Greek mythology with the head and tail of a bull and the body of a man
Q129866.lead: In Greek mythology, the Minotaur, also known as Asterion or Asterius, is a mythical creature portrayed during classical antiquity with the head and tail of a bull and the body of a man or, as described by Roman poet Ovid, a being "part man and part bull". He dwelt at the center of the Labyrinth, which was an elaborate maze-like construction designed by the architect Daedalus and his son Icarus, upon command of King Minos of Crete.

Q130818.label: Atlas
Q130818.lead: In Greek mythology, Atlas is a Titan condemned to hold up the heavens or sky for eternity after the Titanomachy. Atlas also plays a role in the myths of two of the greatest Greek heroes: Heracles (Hercules in Roman mythology) and Perseus.

Q130832.label: Perseus
Q130832.description: legendary Greek hero and founder of Mycenae, demigod son of Zeus and Danae; famous for beheading the Gorgon Medusa
Q130832.lead: In Greek mythology, Perseus is the legendary founder of the Perseid dynasty. He was, alongside Cadmus and Bellerophon, the greatest Greek hero and slayer of monsters before the days of Heracles.

Q130890.label: Oedipus
Q130890.lead: Oedipus was a mythical Greek king of Thebes. A tragic hero in Greek mythology, Oedipus unwittingly fulfilled a prophecy that he would end up killing his father and marrying his mother, thereby bringing disaster to his city and family.

Q131090.label: Chaos
Q131090.lead: In the context of religious cosmogony, Chaos refers to the division of reality outside or in contrast to the ordered cosmos. As such it refers to a state, place, or time beyond the known, familiar, and reliable world, often said to be inhabited by strange, ominous, or demonic beings.

Q131125.label: Hebe
Q131125.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Hebe is the goddess of youth or of the prime of life. She was the cup-bearer for the gods of Mount Olympus, serving their nectar and ambrosia.

Q131346.label: Pandora
Q131346.description: mythological figure, first human woman created by Hephaestus
Q131346.lead: In Greek mythology, Pandora was the first human woman, created by Hephaestus on the instructions of Zeus. As Hesiod related it, each deity cooperated by giving her unique gifts.

Q131351.label: Antigone
Q131351.description: mythical daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta
Q131351.lead: In Greek mythology, Antigone was a Theban princess and a character in several ancient Greek tragedies. She was the daughter of Oedipus, king of Thebes; her mother/grandmother was either Jocasta or, in another variation of the myth, Euryganeia.

Q131445.label: Jocasta
Q131445.lead: In Greek mythology, Jocasta, also rendered as Iocaste and Epicaste (Ἐπικάστη Epikástē), was Queen of Thebes through her marriages to Laius and her son, Oedipus. She is best known for her role in the myths surrounding Oedipus and her eventual suicide upon the discovery of his identity.

Q13156677.label: Butes
Q13156677.description: mythical hero in Athens, son of Pandion

Q131575.label: Hecate
Q131575.lead: Hecate is a goddess in ancient Greek religion and mythology. Variously associated with crossroads, night, light, magic, witchcraft, and the Moon, she is most often shown holding a pair of torches, a key, or snakes, or accompanied by dogs, and in later periods she is typically depicted as three-formed or triple-bodied.

Q131588.label: Ganymede
Q131588.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology
Q131588.lead: In Greek mythology, Ganymede ( GAN-im-eed) or Ganymedes is a divine hero whose homeland was Troy. Homer describes Ganymede as the most handsome of mortals and tells the story of how he was abducted by the gods to serve as Zeus's cup-bearer in Olympus.

Q1320718.label: Theseus
Q1320718.description: legendary king of Athens, son of Aegeus and Aethra; famous for slaying the Minotaur
Q1320718.lead: Theseus was a divine hero in Greek mythology, famous for slaying the Minotaur. The myths surrounding Theseus, his journeys, exploits, and friends, have provided material for storytelling throughout the ages.

Q132582.label: Pan
Q132582.description: Greek god of the mountain wilds, shepherds, flocks, rustic music, fertility, spring, and theatrical criticism, with the hindquarters, legs, and horns of a goat
Q132582.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Pan is the god of the wild, shepherds and flocks, rustic music and impromptus, and companion of the nymphs. He has the hindquarters, legs, and horns of a goat, in the same manner as a faun or satyr.

Q1328260.label: Eleusis
Q1328260.description: eponymous hero of the town of Eleusis
Q1328260.lead: In Greek mythology, Eleusis ( ih-LEW-siss) or Eleusinus was the eponymous hero of the town of Eleusis.

Q1330532.label: Lycomedes
Q1330532.description: king of Scyros in Greek mythology
Q1330532.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycomedes, also known as Lycurgus, was the most prominent king of the Dolopians in the island of Scyros near Euboea during the Trojan War.

Q1332949.label: Manto
Q1332949.lead: In Greek mythology, Manto was a seer from Thebes. She was the daughter of the prophet Tiresias and mother of Mopsus.

Q134270.label: Helios
Q134270.description: Greek god and personification of the Sun
Q134270.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Helios is the god who personifies the Sun. His name is also Latinized as Helius, and he is often given the epithets Hyperion ("the one above") and Phaethon ("the shining").

Q1347046.label: Epicaste
Q1347046.description: figure in Greek mythology, daughter of King Calydon by Aeolia

Q134756.label: Daedalus
Q134756.description: son of Metion in Greek mythology
Q134756.lead: In Greek mythology, Daedalus was a skillful architect and craftsman, seen as a symbol of wisdom, knowledge and power. He is the father of Icarus, the uncle of Perdix, and possibly also the father of Iapyx.

Q1347568.label: Epopeus
Q1347568.lead: In Greek mythology, Epopeus was the 17th king of Sicyon, with an archaic bird-name that linked him to epops (ἔποψ), the hoopoe, the "watcher".

Q1362409.label: Canace
Q1362409.description: daughter of Aiolos in Greek mythology
Q1362409.lead: In Greek mythology, Canace was the daughter of Aeolus, the king of Thessaly, and Enarete, daughter of Deimachus. She is known for the story, told by Euripides and Ovid, of her incestuous relationship with her brother Macareus and her subsequent suicide.

Q1371026.label: Eteoclus
Q1371026.description: son of Iphis in Greek mythology
Q1371026.lead: In Greek mythology, Eteoclus was the son of Iphis.

Q1378407.label: Euryalus
Q1378407.description: son of Mecisteus in Greek Mythology

Q1378556.label: Eurypylus
Q1378556.description: son of Poseidon and king of Cos
Q1378556.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurypylus was a king of the island of Cos.

Q1395752.label: Teuthras
Q1395752.lead: In Greek mythology, Teuthras was a king of Mysia, and mythological eponym of the town of Teuthrania.

Q1411680.label: Pleuron
Q1411680.lead: In Greek mythology, Pleuron was a son of Aetolus and Pronoe, daughter of Phorbus, and brother of Calydon. He was married to Xanthippe, daughter of Dorus, by whom he became the father of Agenor, Sterope, Stratonice, and Laophonte.

Q1415180.label: Scylla
Q1415180.description: Greek mythological figure, daughter of Nisos
Q1415180.lead: In Greek mythology, Scylla was a princess of Megara as daughter of King Nisus.

Q1419140.label: Opheltes
Q1419140.description: son of Lycurgus of Nemea in Greek mythology
Q1419140.lead: In Greek mythology, Opheltes, also called Archemorus (Αρχέμορος, Beginning of Doom), was a son of Lycurgus of Nemea. His mother is variously given as Eurydice, Nemea, or Amphithea.

Q1421201.label: Porphyrion
Q1421201.lead: In Greek mythology, Porphyrion was one of the Gigantes (Giants), who according to Hesiod, were the offspring of Gaia, born from the blood that fell when Uranus (Sky) was castrated by their son Cronus. In some other versions of the myth, the Gigantes were born of Gaia and Tartarus.

Q1424817.label: Pterelaus
Q1424817.lead: In Greek mythology, Pterelaus was a king of the Taphians.

Q142739.label: Alcaeus
Q142739.description: son of Perseus in Greek mythology

Q143880.label: Athamas
Q143880.description: son of Minyas or Aeolus in Greek mythology
Q143880.lead: In Greek mythology, Athamas was a Boeotian king.

Q1455747.label: Hippomenes
Q1455747.lead: The name Hippomenes may also refer to the father of Leimone. In Greek mythology, Hippomenes is a Boeotian prince, the son of Megareus.

Q1456409.label: Iobates
Q1456409.description: character in Greek mythology, Lycian king
Q1456409.lead: In Greek mythology, Iobates or Jobates is a Lycian king, the father of Antea and Philonoe. He was sometimes named Amphianax.

Q1462644.label: Learchus
Q1462644.description: son of Athamas in Greek mythology
Q1462644.lead: In Greek mythology, Learchus or Learches was the son of King Athamas and Ino, daughter of King Cadmus of Thebes. He was the brother of Melicertes.

Q1469456.label: Metanira
Q1469456.lead: In Greek mythology, Metanira or Meganira was a queen of Eleusis as wife of King Celeus. She was the daughter of Amphictyon, the king of Athens.

Q1471633.label: Aloeus
Q1471633.description: Greek mythical character, son of Poseidon

Q148030.label: Triton
Q148030.description: Greek god, messenger of the sea
Q148030.lead: Triton is a Greek god of the sea, the son of Poseidon and Amphitrite. Triton lived with his parents in a golden palace on the bottom of the sea.

Q1495743.label: Ilus
Q1495743.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology, mythological founder of Troy
Q1495743.lead: In Greek mythology, Ilus was the founder of the city called Ilios or Ilion (Latinized as Ilium) to which he gave his name. When the latter became the chief city of the Trojan people it was also often called Troy, the name by which it is best known today.

Q152262.label: Pluto
Q152262.description: god in Roman religion, Plouton in Greek
Q152262.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Pluto was the ruler of the underworld. The earlier name for the god was Hades, which became more common as the name of the underworld itself.

Q1536527.label: Aleus
Q1536527.description: in mythology, the king of Arcadia
Q1536527.lead: In Greek mythology, Aleus (or Aleos) was the king of Arcadia, eponym of Alea, and founder of the cult of Athena Alea. He was the grandson of Arcas.

Q1538212.label: Gorge
Q1538212.description: figure in Greek mythology (daughter of Oeneus and Althaea)

Q1539620.label: Oeagrus
Q1539620.lead: In Greek mythology, Oeagrus was a king of Thrace, and father of Orpheus.

Q1568394.label: Idaea
Q1568394.description: daughter of Dardanus (Scythian king) in Greek mythology
Q1568394.lead: Idaea or Idaia referring to either the Cretan Mount Ida, or the Phrygian Mount Ida in the Troad, is the name of several figures in Greek mythology: Idaea, a nymph, who was the mother, by the river-god Scamander, of King Teucer. Idaea, the daughter of the Scythian king Dardanus, and wife of Phineus, who falsely accused her stepsons, leading to their imprisonment and torture.

Q15721.label: Python
Q15721.description: dragon of Delphi killed by the god Apollo
Q15721.lead: In Greek mythology, Python was the serpent, sometimes represented as a medieval-style dragon, living at the center of the Earth, believed by the ancient Greeks to be at Delphi.

Q159168.label: Themis
Q159168.description: in ancient Greek mythology, a titaness, the personification of divine order, fairness, law, natural law, and custom, whose symbols are the scales of justice
Q159168.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Themis is the goddess and personification of justice, divine order, law, and custom. She is one of the twelve Titan children of Gaia and Uranus, and the second wife of Zeus.

Q159666.label: Hector
Q159666.description: prince of Troy in Greek mythology
Q159666.lead: In Greek mythology, Hector was a Trojan prince, a hero, and the greatest warrior for Troy during the Trojan War. He is a major character in Homer's Iliad, where he leads the Trojans and their allies in the defense of Troy, killing countless Greek warriors.

Q1601938.label: Laodamia
Q1601938.description: Greek mythology character, daughter of Bellerophon

Q160730.label: Medusa
Q160730.description: in Greek mythology, one of the three Gorgons, described as a woman with snakes in place of hair, beheaded by Perseus
Q160730.lead: In Greek mythology, Medusa, also called Gorgo (Ancient Greek: Γοργώ) or the Gorgon, was one of the three Gorgons. Medusa is generally described as a woman with living snakes in place of hair; her appearance was so hideous that anyone who looked upon her was turned to stone.

Q161419.label: Oceanus
Q161419.description: ancient Greek god of the earth-encircling river, Oceanos
Q161419.lead: In Greek mythology, Oceanus or Okeanos was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), and the god of the great river which encircled the entire world. He was the brother and husband of the Titaness Tethys, and by her was the father of the river gods and the Oceanids.

Q161582.label: Andromeda
Q161582.lead: In Greek mythology, Andromeda is the daughter of Cepheus, the king of Aethiopia, and his wife, Cassiopeia. When Cassiopeia boasts that she (or Andromeda) is more beautiful than the Nereids, Poseidon sends the sea monster Cetus to ravage the coast of Aethiopia as divine punishment.

Q1620067.label: Hippothoe
Q1620067.description: daughter of Mestor in Greek mythology

Q162797.label: Pegasus
Q162797.lead: Pegasus is a winged horse in Greek mythology, usually depicted as a white stallion. He was sired by Poseidon, in his role as horse-god, and foaled by Medusa, one of three Gorgon sisters.

Q1636827.label: Pelasgus
Q1636827.description: ancestor of the Arcadians in Greek mythology

Q163920.label: Adonis
Q163920.description: Greek god of beauty and desire
Q163920.lead: In Greek mythology, Adonis was the mortal lover of the goddesses Aphrodite and Persephone. He was considered to be the ideal of male beauty in classical antiquity.

Q1640434.label: Alcippe
Q1640434.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcippe is daughter of Ares and the mortal princess Aglauros.

Q164061.label: Helen of Troy
Q164061.description: daughter of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q164061.lead: Helen, commonly known as Helen of Troy and sometimes as Helen of Sparta, is a figure in Greek mythology said to have been the most beautiful woman in the world. She was believed to have been the daughter of Zeus by Leda or Nemesis, and the sister of Clytemnestra, Castor, Pollux, Philonoe, Phoebe and Timandra.

Q1641282.label: Zeuxippe
Q1641282.description: spouse of the legendary Athenian king Pandion I

Q1643451.label: Alecto
Q1643451.description: one of the Erinyes or Furies, ancient Greek mythological punisher of moral crimes
Q1643451.lead: Alecto is one of the Erinyes or Furies in classical mythology, primarily in Roman mythology.

Q16515493.label: Amphidamas
Q16515493.description: in Greek mythology son of Busiris killed by Heracles

Q165170.label: Europa
Q165170.description: Phoenician character in Greek mythology, daughter of Agenor
Q165170.lead: In Greek mythology, Europa was a Phoenician princess said to have been abducted by Zeus in the form of a bull. She was the mother of the Cretan king Minos.

Q165769.label: Penelope
Q165769.description: wife of Odysseus in Greek mythology
Q165769.lead: Penelope is the legendary wife of Odysseus and queen of Ithaca in Homer's Odyssey. She is the daughter of Spartan king Icarius, and the mother of Telemachus.

Q16641710.label: Herse
Q16641710.lead: Herse was a figure in Greek mythology, the Athenian princess as the daughter of King Cecrops of Athens and Aglaurus, daughter of King Actaeus.

Q16671639.label: Pyrene
Q16671639.description: mythological character, mother of Cycnos and lover of Ares

Q1675360.label: Itys
Q1675360.lead: In Greek mythology, Itys is a minor mythological Thracian character, the son of Tereus, a king of Thrace, by his Athenian wife Procne. Itys was murdered by his own mother and aunt and served to be consumed during dinner by his father, as part of a revenge plan against Tereus for assaulting and raping the maiden Philomela, Procne's sister.

Q1676297.label: Pteleon
Q1676297.description: lover of Procris in Greek mythology

Q167646.label: Paris
Q167646.description: mythological son of Priam, king of Troy
Q167646.lead: Paris, also known as Alexander (Ancient Greek: Ἀλέξανδρος, romanized: Aléxandros), is a figure from Greek mythology who appears in the numerous stories about the Trojan War, including the Iliad. He was prince of Troy, son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba, and younger brother of Prince Hector.

Q16931911.label: Pandion
Q16931911.description: eponymous hero of the Attic tribe Pandionis
Q16931911.lead: Pandion was the eponymous hero of the Attic tribe Pandionis, which was created as part of the tribal reforms of Cleisthenes at the end of the sixth century BC. He is usually assumed to be one of the two legendary kings of Athens, Pandion I or Pandion II.

Q170473.label: Priam
Q170473.description: the legendary and last king of Troy during the Trojan war; son of Laomedon
Q170473.lead: In Greek mythology, Priam was the legendary and last king of Troy during the Trojan War. He was the son of Laomedon.

Q1705660.label: Heleus
Q1705660.description: son of Perseus in Greek mythology
Q1705660.lead: In Greek mythology, Heleus or Heleius, also Helios (Ἕλιος), was a Mycenaean prince.

Q170779.label: Cassandra
Q170779.description: mythological prophetess and princess of Troy
Q170779.lead: In Greek mythology, Cassandra, also spelled Kassandra or Casandra, was a Trojan priestess dedicated to the god Apollo and fated by him to utter true prophecies, but never to be believed. Cassandra lived through the Trojan War and survived the sack of the city, but was murdered by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus when Agamemnon brought her to Mycenae as a pallake.

Q171839.label: Menelaus
Q171839.description: mythical king of Sparta, husband of Helen of Troy
Q171839.lead: In Greek mythology, Menelaus was a king of Sparta. According to the Iliad, the Trojan War began as a result of Menelaus' wife, Helen, fleeing to Troy with the Trojan prince Paris.

Q1722780.label: Calydon
Q1722780.description: son of Aetolus in Greek mythology
Q1722780.lead: In Greek mythology, Calydon was the eponymous ruler of Calydon, a city in Aetolia.

Q1722781.label: Calyce
Q1722781.description: daughter of Aiolos in Greek mythology

Q172725.label: Ajax the Great
Q172725.description: son of Telamon in Greek mythology
Q172725.lead: Ajax or Aias is a Greek mythological hero, the son of King Telamon and Periboea, and the half-brother of Teucer.

Q174278.label: Medea
Q174278.description: daughter of King Aeëtes of Colchis in Greek mythology
Q174278.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Medea is the daughter of King Aeëtes of Colchis. Medea is known in most stories as a sorceress, an accomplished pharmakís, a worker in pharmakeía (medicinal magic), and is often depicted as a high priestess of the goddess Hecate.

Q174353.label: Orpheus
Q174353.description: legendary musician, poet, and prophet in ancient Greek religion and myth
Q174353.lead: In Greek mythology, Orpheus was a Thracian bard, legendary musician and prophet. He was also a renowned poet and, according to legend, travelled with Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece, and descended into the underworld to recover his lost wife, Eurydice.

Q176130.label: Campe
Q176130.lead: In Greek mythology, Campe, Kampe, or Kampê was a female monster. She was the guard, in Tartarus, of the Cyclopes and Hecatoncheires, whom Uranus had imprisoned there.

Q176758.label: Jason
Q176758.description: Greek mythological hero, son of Aeson
Q176758.lead: Jason was an ancient Greek mythological hero and leader of the Argonauts, whose quest for the Golden Fleece is featured in Greek literature. He was the son of Aeson, the rightful king of Iolcos.

Q1774178.label: Cleopatra
Q1774178.description: Greek mythological person, daughter of Idas and Marpessa
Q1774178.lead: In Greek mythology Cleopatra, sometimes called Alcyone (Ancient Greek: Ἀλκυόνη, romanized: Alkuónē, lit. 'kingfisher') was the daughter of Idas and Marpessa and the wife of Meleager, a Calydonian prince and participant in the Calydonian boar hunt. Together they had a daughter, Polydora.

Q1779164.label: Phyleus
Q1779164.lead: In Greek mythology, Phyleus was an Elean prince and one of the Calydonian boar hunters.

Q1784645.label: Coronus
Q1784645.description: Greek mythical character, son of Caeneus

Q178641.label: Peleus
Q178641.description: son of Aeacus in Greek mythology
Q178641.lead: In Greek mythology, Peleus was a hero, king of Phthia, husband of Thetis and the father of their son Achilles.

Q1788026.label: Cresphontes
Q1788026.description: king of Messenia in Greek mythology
Q1788026.lead: In Greek mythology, Cresphontes was a son of Aristomachus, husband of Merope, father of Aepytus and brother of Temenus and Aristodemus. He was a great-great-grandson of Heracles and helped lead the fifth and final attack on Mycenae in the Peloponnesus.

Q178831.label: Aurora
Q178831.description: goddess of dawn in Roman mythology
Q178831.lead: In Roman mythology, Aurora is the goddess and personification of the dawn. Aurora is the Latin word for dawn, and she appeared frequently in Latin literature.

Q179014.label: Io
Q179014.description: nymph seduced by Zeus in Greek mythology
Q179014.lead: In Greek mythology, Io was one of the mortal lovers of Zeus. An Argive princess, her descendants included Perseus, Cadmus, Heracles, Minos, Lynceus, Cepheus, Dionysus, and Danaus.

Q1790716.label: Iambe
Q1790716.description: Thracian mythological character who entertained Demeter
Q1790716.lead: Iambe, in Greek mythology, was a Thracian woman, daughter of Pan and Echo, granddaughter of Hermes, and a servant of Metaneira, the wife of Hippothoon. Others call her a slave of Celeus, king of Eleusis.

Q179209.label: Hyperion
Q179209.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyperion was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). With his sister, the Titaness Theia, Hyperion fathered Helios (Sun), Selene (Moon) and Eos (Dawn).

Q1795211.label: Cyzicus
Q1795211.description: Greek mythical character, King of the Doliones
Q1795211.lead: In Greek mythology, King Cyzicus or Kyzikos was the ruler of the Dolionians, a tribe that inhabited the southern shore of the Propontis (the Sea of Marmara). He gave his name to a city of the same name, Cyzicus, his capital.

Q179543.label: Iapetos
Q179543.lead: In Greek mythology, Iapetus or Iapetos, also Japetus or Japetos, was one of the Titans, the son of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth) and father of Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus, and Menoetius. He was also called the father of Buphagus and Anchiale in other sources.

Q17996944.label: Tmolus
Q17996944.description: King of Lydia and husband to Omphale in Greek mythology
Q17996944.lead: In Greek mythology, Tmolus may refer to the following figures: Tmolus, a king of Lydia and the husband of Omphale, to whom he bequeathed his kingdom. Tmolus, the god of Mount Tmolus in Lydia, who was the judge of a musical contest between the gods Apollo and Pan (or the satyr Marsyas).

Q180222.label: Amphitrite
Q180222.description: Oceanid or Nereid of Greek mythology
Q180222.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Amphitrite was the goddess of the sea, the queen of the sea, and her consort is Poseidon. She was a daughter of Nereus and Doris (or Oceanus and Tethys).

Q180237.label: Typhon
Q180237.lead: Typhon, also known as Typhoeus (Τυφωεύς, Typhōeús), Typhaon (Τυφάων, Typháōn) or Typhos (Τυφώς, Typhṓs), was a monstrous serpentine giant and one of the deadliest creatures in Greek mythology. According to Hesiod, Typhon was the son of Gaia and Tartarus.

Q180287.label: Moirae
Q180287.description: personifications of fate in Greek mythology
Q180287.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, the Moirai—often known in English as the Fates—were the personifications of destiny. In certain accounts, they were considered as three sisters: Clotho (the spinner), Lachesis (the allotter), and Atropos (the inevitable, a metaphor for death), though their number and names varied over time according to the author.

Q182019.label: Leda
Q182019.description: daughter of Thestius in Greek mythology
Q182019.lead: In Greek mythology, Leda, also rendered as Lede, was an Aetolian princess who became queen consort of Sparta through her marriage to King Tyndareus. Zeus fell in love with Leda, and to avoid his wife Hera's jealousy, assaulted her while disguised as a swan.

Q182101.label: Tantalus
Q182101.description: son of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q182101.lead: Tantalus, was a Greek mythological figure, most famous for his punishment in Tartarus: for either revealing many secrets of the gods, for stealing ambrosia from them, or for trying to trick them into eating his son, he was made to stand in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree with low branches, with the fruit ever eluding his grasp, and the water always receding before he could take a drink. This punishment, although the best-known today, was a more unusual detail in surviving early Greek sources, where variants including a stone suspended above his head are more commonly recorded.

Q182439.label: Pelias
Q182439.description: mythical king of Iolcus, and son of Poseidon who sent Jason on the quest for the Golden Fleece
Q182439.lead: Pelias was king of Iolcus in Greek mythology. He was the one who sent Jason on the quest for the Golden Fleece.

Q182837.label: Coeus
Q182837.description: Titan in Greek mythology, one of the twelve titans
Q182837.lead: In Greek mythology, Coeus, also called Koios or Polus, was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth).

Q183417.label: Chiron
Q183417.lead: In Greek mythology, Chiron, also Cheiron or Kheiron, was held to be the superlative centaur amongst his brethren since he was called the "wisest and justest of all the centaurs".

Q184216.label: Tethys
Q184216.description: ancient Greek mythological figure; mother of the river gods and the Oceanids
Q184216.lead: In Greek mythology, Tethys was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), the sister and wife of the Titan Oceanus, and the mother of the river gods and the Oceanids. Although Tethys had no active role in Greek mythology and no established cults, she was depicted in mosaics decorating baths, pools, and triclinia in the Greek East, particularly in Antioch and its suburbs, either alone or with Oceanus.

Q184437.label: Thetis
Q184437.lead: Thetis is a figure from Greek mythology with varying mythological roles. She mainly appears as a sea nymph, a goddess of water, and one of the 50 Nereids, daughters of the ancient sea god Nereus.

Q184570.label: Iris
Q184570.description: the personification of the rainbow in ancient Greek religion and mythology
Q184570.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Iris is a daughter of the gods Thaumas and Electra, and the personification of the rainbow. She functions as a messenger and servant to the Olympians, particularly Hera.

Q1851846.label: Medus
Q1851846.description: son of Medea with either Aegeas or Jason
Q1851846.lead: In Greek mythology, Medus, also Medeus or Medeius (Μήδειος, Mḗdeios, lit. 'son of Medea', 'from Media', 'Median' or 'appertaining to the Medes'), was an Athenian prince as the son of King Aegeus, thus a half-brother of the hero Theseus.

Q18551588.label: Otus
Q18551588.description: mythological giant son of Poseidon or Aloeus

Q185670.label: Echidna
Q185670.description: ancient Greek mythological monster, the mother of monsters
Q185670.lead: In Greek mythology, Echidna was a monster, half-woman and half-snake, who lived alone in a cave. She was the mate of the fearsome monster Typhon and was the mother of many of the most famous monsters of Greek myth.

Q186271.label: Patroclus
Q186271.description: son of Menoetius in Greek mythology, a greek hero of the Trojan war
Q186271.lead: Patroclus was a Greek hero of the Trojan War and close companion of the hero Achilles in Greek mythology. Patroclus is an important character in Homer's Iliad.

Q18642285.label: Asteria
Q18642285.description: daughter of the Titans Coeus and Phoebe and sister of Leto
Q18642285.lead: In Greek mythology, Asteria or Asterie is a daughter of the Titans Phoebe and Coeus (Polus) and the sister of Leto. According to Hesiod, by the Titan Perses she had a single child, a daughter named Hecate, the goddess of witchcraft.

Q187602.label: Circe
Q187602.lead: In Greek mythology, Circe is a witch and goddess. In most accounts, Circe is described as a daughter of the sun god Helios and the Oceanid Perse.

Q1886507.label: Merope
Q1886507.description: daughter of Cypselus of Arcadia in Greek mythology
Q1886507.lead: Merope was a Queen of Messenia in Greek mythology, daughter of King Cypselus of Arcadia and wife of Cresphontes, the Heraclid king of Messenia. After the murder of her husband and her two older children by Polyphontes (another Heraclid), Merope was forced to marry the murderer, but she managed to save her youngest son Aepytus, whom she sent secretly to Aetolia.

Q189527.label: Nereus
Q189527.lead: In Greek mythology, Nereus was the eldest son of Pontus (the Sea) and Gaia (the Earth). Nereus and Doris became the parents of 50 daughters (the Nereids) and a son (Nerites), with whom Nereus lived in the Aegean Sea.

Q189872.label: Bellerophon
Q189872.description: Hero in Greek myth who rode Pegasus and killed the Chimera
Q189872.lead: Bellerophon or Bellerophontes or Hipponous (Ancient Greek: Ἱππόνοος, lit. 'horse-knower'), was a divine Corinthian hero of Greek mythology, the son of Poseidon and Eurynome, and the foster son of Glaukos. He was "the greatest hero and slayer of monsters, alongside Cadmus and Perseus, before the days of Heracles".

Q190103.label: Castor and Pollux
Q190103.lead: Castor and Pollux (or Polydeuces) are twin half-brothers in Greek and Roman mythology, known together as the Dioscuri or Dioskouroi. Their mother was Leda, but they had different fathers; Castor was the mortal son of Tyndareus, the king of Sparta, while Pollux was the divine son of Zeus, who seduced Leda in the guise of a swan.

Q190323.label: Atalanta
Q190323.description: Greek mythological character, the only female Argonaut
Q190323.lead: Atalanta is a heroine in Greek mythology. There are two versions of the huntress Atalanta: one from Arcadia, whose parents were Iasus and Clymene and who is primarily known from the tales of the Calydonian boar hunt and the Argonauts; and the other from Boeotia, who is the daughter of King Schoeneus and is primarily noted for her skill in the footrace.

Q190543.label: Alkmene
Q190543.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcmene or Alcmena ( alk-MEE-nə; Doric Greek: Ἀλκμάνα, romanized: Alkmána; Latin: Alcumena; meaning "strong in wrath") was the wife of Amphitryon, by whom she bore two children, Iphicles and Laonome. She is best known as the mother of Heracles, whose father was the god Zeus.

Q190563.label: Pontus
Q190563.lead: In Greek mythology, Pontus is the personification of the sea. In Hesiod's Theogony (8th or 7th century BC), he is the offspring of Gaia (the Earth), who produces him alone.

Q190565.label: Metis
Q190565.description: Oceanid of Greek mythology, goddess of wisdom, daughter of Oceanid and Tethys
Q190565.lead: Metis, in ancient Greek religion and mythology, was the pre-Olympian goddess of wisdom, counsel and deep thought, and a member of the Oceanids. She is notable for being the advisor and first wife of Zeus, the king of the gods.

Q191481.label: Proteus
Q191481.lead: In Greek mythology, Proteus is an early prophetic sea god or god of rivers and oceanic bodies of water, one of several deities whom Homer calls the "Old Man of the Sea" (hálios gérôn). Some who ascribe a specific domain to Proteus call him the god of "elusive sea change", which suggests the changeable nature of the sea or the liquid quality of water.

Q191725.label: Aegeus
Q191725.lead: Aegeus was one of the kings of Athens in Greek mythology, who gave his name to the Aegean Sea, was the father of Theseus, and founded Athenian institutions.

Q1920680.label: Menoetius
Q1920680.description: son of Actor and father of Patroclus

Q192109.label: Admetus
Q192109.description: king of Pherae in Thessaly, in Greek mythology
Q192109.lead: In Greek mythology, Admetus was a king of Pherae in Thessaly.

Q192136.label: Kreios
Q192136.description: Titan in Greek mythology, name that means ram
Q192136.lead: In Greek mythology, Crius, Krios or Kreios was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth).

Q192407.label: Orestes
Q192407.description: son of Agamemnon in Greek mythology
Q192407.lead: In Greek mythology, Orestes or Orestis was the son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, and the brother of Electra and Iphigenia. He was also known by the patronymic Agamemnonides (Ἀγαμεμνονίδης), meaning "son of Agamemnon." He is the subject of multiple Ancient Greek plays (including Aeschylus' Oresteia), which depict his revenge, madness, and ritual purification.

Q1924653.label: Meta
Q1924653.description: Greek mythological figure, daughter of Hoples and first wife of Aegeus
Q1924653.lead: In Greek mythology, Meta was the daughter of Hoples, son of Ion, Eponym of the Ionians. In other traditions, Meta was called Melite.

Q192469.label: Atreus
Q192469.description: king of Mycenae, father of Agamemnon
Q192469.lead: In Greek mythology, Atreus was a king of Mycenae in the Peloponnese, the son of Pelops and Hippodamia, and the father of Agamemnon and Menelaus. His descendants became known collectively as the Atreidae (Ancient Greek: Ἀτρείδαι Atreidai).

Q192485.label: Pelops
Q192485.description: son of Tantalus in Greek mythology, king of Pisa in the Peloponnesus region
Q192485.lead: In Greek mythology, Pelops was king of Pisa in the Peloponnesus region (Πελοπόννησος, lit. "Pelops's Island").

Q192946.label: Tyndareus
Q192946.lead: In Greek mythology, Tyndareus was a Spartan king.

Q193267.label: Nestor
Q193267.description: wise ruler of Pylos in Greek mythology, son of Neleus
Q193267.lead: In Greek mythology, Nestor of Gerenia was a legendary king of Pylos. He is a prominent secondary character in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, where he appears as an elderly warrior who frequently offers advice to the other characters.

Q193433.label: Hecuba
Q193433.lead: In Greek mythology, Hecuba was the wife of King Priam and queen of Troy during the Trojan War. With Priam, she was the mother of the warriors Hector and Troilus; Helen's suitor Paris; and the prophetess Cassandra.

Q193609.label: Rhadamanthus
Q193609.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa
Q193609.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhadamanthus or Rhadamanthys was a wise king of Crete. As the son of Zeus and Europa he was considered a demigod.

Q19376.label: Andromache
Q19376.description: wife of Hector in Greek mythology
Q19376.lead: In Greek mythology, Andromache was the wife of Hector, daughter of Eetion, and sister to Podes. She was born and raised in the city of Cilician Thebe, over which her father ruled.

Q1943680.label: Molus
Q1943680.description: mythical son of Deucalion or Minos
Q1943680.lead: In Greek mythology, Molus was the illegitimate son of Deucalion, son of Minos, king of Crete or of Minos instead.

Q196865.label: Zethos
Q196865.lead: Amphion and Zethus (Ancient Greek: Ζῆθος, romanized: Zêthos) were, in ancient Greek mythology, the twin sons of Zeus (or Theobus) by Antiope. They are important characters in one of the two founding myths of the city of Thebes, because they constructed the city's walls.

Q19738771.label: Arethusa
Q19738771.description: one of the Hesperides in Greek mythology

Q199923.label: Dione
Q199923.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Dione is an oracular goddess and Titaness. She is primarily known from Book V of Homer's Iliad, where she tends to the wounds suffered by her daughter Aphrodite.

Q20018046.label: Capys
Q20018046.description: son of Assaracus in Greek mythology
Q20018046.lead: In Roman and Greek mythology, Capys was a king of Dardania during the Iliad and Aeneid.

Q200382.label: Phorcys
Q200382.lead: In Greek mythology, Phorcys or Phorcus is a primordial sea god, generally cited (first in Hesiod) as the son of Pontus and Gaia (Earth). Classical scholar Karl Kerenyi conflated Phorcys with the similar sea gods Nereus and Proteus.

Q201261.label: Orion
Q201261.lead: In Greek mythology, Orion was a giant huntsman whom Zeus or Artemis placed among the stars as a constellation. He was venerated as a hero in the region of Boeotia, and there is one etiological passage which says that Orion was responsible for the present shape of the Strait of Sicily.

Q2026930.label: Opis
Q2026930.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Upis or Opis (Ancient Greek: Ὦπις, romanized: Ôpis) is a maiden from Hyperborea, a daughter of the wind-god Boreas. Upis along with her sisters descended from Hyperborea and went to the island of Delos, where they became handmaidens to the goddess Artemis.

Q203673.label: Callisto
Q203673.lead: In Greek mythology, Callisto was a nymph (an Arcadian mountain nymph; an Oread), or the daughter of King Lycaon; the myth varies in such details. She was believed to be one of the followers of Artemis (Diana for the Romans) who was pursued by Zeus.

Q205233.label: Maia
Q205233.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Maia, also spelled Maie, is one of the Pleiades and the mother of the messenger god Hermes by Zeus. Maia was identified with the Roman earth goddess Maia, the mother of Mercury.

Q206187.label: Aeacus
Q206187.description: son of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q206187.lead: Aeacus was a king of the island of Aegina in Greek mythology. He was a son of Zeus and the nymph Aegina, and the father of the heroes Peleus and Telamon.

Q206214.label: Amphitryon
Q206214.description: figure in Greek mythology, husband of Alcmene
Q206214.lead: Amphitryon, in Greek mythology, was a son of Alcaeus, king of Tiryns in Argolis. His mother was named either Astydameia, the daughter of Pelops and Hippodamia, or Laonome, daughter of Guneus, or else Hipponome, daughter of Menoeceus.

Q2067646.label: Pisidice
Q2067646.description: Greek mythical character, daughter of Aeolus

Q2070945.label: Perimede
Q2070945.description: daughter of Aiolos in Greek mythology

Q207273.label: Hyacinth
Q207273.lead: Hyacinth or Hyacinthus is a deified hero and a lover of Apollo in Greek mythology. His cult at Amyclae southwest of Sparta dates from the Mycenaean era.

Q207663.label: Augeias of Elis
Q207663.description: son of Phorbas in Greek mythology
Q207663.lead: In Greek mythology, Augeas, also called Aegeus, was king of Elis and father of Epicaste. Some ancient authors say that Augeas was one of the Argonauts.

Q207681.label: Cassiopeia
Q207681.description: figure in Greek mythology; queen of Aethiopia and wife of king Cepheus
Q207681.lead: Cassiopeia, also variously spelled as Cassiope (Ancient Greek: Κασσιόπη, romanized: Kassiópē) or Cassiepeia (Ancient Greek: Κασσιέπεια, romanized: Kassiépeia), is a figure in Greek and Roman mythology, the queen of Aethiopia and wife of King Cepheus. She was arrogant and vain, characteristics that led to the endangerment of her daughter Andromeda and her own downfall.

Q207715.label: Deucalion
Q207715.description: son of Prometheus in Greek mythology
Q207715.lead: In Greek mythology, Deucalion was the son of Prometheus; ancient sources name his mother as Clymene, Hesione, or Pronoia. He is closely connected with a flood myth in Greek mythology.

Q208017.label: Acrisius
Q208017.lead: In Greek mythology, Acrisius was a king of Argos. He was the grandfather of the famous Greek demi-god Perseus through his only daughter Danaë.

Q208531.label: Actaeon
Q208531.description: son of Aristaeus in Greek mythology
Q208531.lead: In Greek mythology, Actaeon was the son of the priestly herdsman Aristaeus in Boeotia, and a famous Theban hero. Through his mother Autonoë he was a member of the ruling House of Cadmus.

Q208588.label: Eurydice
Q208588.description: oak nymph, or daughter of Apollo and wife of Orpheus
Q208588.lead: Eurydice was a character in Greek mythology and the wife of Orpheus, whom Orpheus tried to bring back from the dead with his enchanting music.

Q209489.label: Ceto
Q209489.lead: Ceto is a primordial sea goddess in Greek mythology, the daughter of Pontus and his mother, Gaia. As a mythological figure, she is considered to be one of the most ancient deities, and bore a host of monstrous children fathered by Phorcys, another child of Gaia and Pontus.

Q2099433.label: Plexippus
Q2099433.description: son of Phineus in Greek mythology

Q2108224.label: Praxithea
Q2108224.description: daughter of Phrasimus or the river-god Cephissus, married to king Erechtheus of Athens

Q210883.label: Danaus
Q210883.lead: In Greek mythology, Danaus was the king of Libya. His myth is a foundation legend of Argos, one of the foremost Mycenaean cities of the Peloponnesus.

Q211953.label: Anchises
Q211953.description: father of Aeneas in Greek mythology, lover of Aphrodite
Q211953.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Anchises was a member of the royal family of Troy. He was said to have been the son of King Capys of Dardania and Themiste, daughter of Ilus, who was son of Tros.

Q212087.label: Eurystheus
Q212087.description: king of Mycenae in Greek mythology
Q212087.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurystheus was king of Tiryns, one of three Mycenaean strongholds in the Argolid, although other authors including Homer and Euripides cast him as ruler of Argos.

Q21272233.label: Bucolion
Q21272233.description: son of Laomedon in Greek mythology
Q21272233.lead: Bucolion may refer to the following: Bucolion, an Arcadian prince as one of the 50 sons of the impious King Lycaon either by the naiad Cyllene, Nonacris or by unknown woman. He and his siblings were the most nefarious and carefree of all people.

Q212827.label: Philoctetes
Q212827.lead: Philoctetes or Philocthetes, according to Greek mythology, was the son of Poeas, king of Meliboea in Thessaly, and Demonassa or Methone. He was a Greek hero, famed as an archer, and a participant in the Trojan War.

Q21567935.label: Pierus
Q21567935.description: king of Emathia, father of the Pierides, eponym of Pieria
Q21567935.lead: In Greek mythology, Pierus was the king of Emathia in Macedonia. He was the eponym of Pieria and Mt.

Q2196048.label: Creusa
Q2196048.lead: In Greek mythology, Creusa was an Athenian princess.

Q221925.label: Acarnan
Q221925.description: son of Alcmaeon in Greek mythology
Q221925.lead: In Greek mythology, Acarnan was son of Alcmaeon and Callirrhoe, and brother of Amphoterus.

Q223152.label: Adrastus
Q223152.lead: In Greek mythology, Adrastus or Adrestus was a king of Argos, and leader of the Seven against Thebes. He was the son of the Argive king Talaus, but was forced out of Argos by his dynastic rival Amphiaraus.

Q223690.label: Ino
Q223690.lead: In Greek mythology, Ino was a Theban princess who later became a queen of Boeotia. After her death and transfiguration, she was worshiped as a goddess under her epithet Leucothea, the "white goddess." Alcman called her "Queen of the Sea" (Ancient Greek: θαλασσομέδουσα, romanized: thalassomédousa), which, if not hyperbole, would make her a goddess parallel to Amphitrite.

Q2293816.label: Endeïs
Q2293816.description: daughter of Sciron in Greek mythology
Q2293816.lead: In Greek mythology, Queen Endeïs was the wife of King Aeacus and mother of the heroes Telamon and Peleus (since Peleus was the father of Achilles and Telamon was the father of Ajax the Great and Teucer, Endeïs was the grandmother of Achilles, Ajax and Teucer). The name is a dialect variant of Engaios (Ἐγγαῖος, "in the earth").

Q23162.label: Asterios
Q23162.description: King of Crete and husband of Europa
Q23162.lead: In Greek mythology, Asterion or Asterius (Ἀστέριος) was a King of Crete and the foster-father of Minos.

Q23168.label: Minos
Q23168.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa, king of Crete
Q23168.lead: In Greek mythology, Minos was a king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa. Every nine years, he made King Aegeus pick seven young boys and seven young girls to be sent to Daedalus's creation, the labyrinth, to be eaten by the Minotaur.

Q2316900.label: Leucippus
Q2316900.description: son of Perieres and father of the Leucippides
Q2316900.lead: In Greek mythology, Leucippus was a Messenian prince. The Boeotian town of Leuctra is said to have derived its name from him.

Q2329005.label: Phegeus
Q2329005.lead: In Greek mythology, Phegeus was the king of Psophis in Arcadia who purified Alcmaeon after the murder of his own mother, Eriphyle. The town of Phegeia, which had before been called Erymanthus, was believed to have derived its name from him.

Q2335647.label: Licymnius
Q2335647.description: son of Electryon in Greek mythology
Q2335647.lead: In Greek mythology, Licymnius was a good friend of Heracles and an illegitimate son of Electryon, King of Tiryns and Mycenae in the Argolid (which makes him half-brother of Alcmene, mother of Heracles). His mother is given as Mideia, a Phrygian woman.

Q2335996.label: Polyeidos
Q2335996.description: mythical seer, who revived Glaucus son of Minos
Q2335996.lead: In Greek mythology, Polyidus also known as Polyeidus, is the son of Coeranus, and a famous seer from Argos or Corinth.

Q241971.label: Aeëtes
Q241971.description: son of Helios in Greek mythology
Q241971.lead: Aeëtes, or Aeeta, was the ruler of the eponymous realm of Aea in Greek mythology, a wondrous realm which from the fifth century B.C.E. onward became identified with the kingdom of Colchis east in the Black Sea. The name comes from the ancient Greek word αἰετός (aietós, "eagle").

Q242835.label: Amphion
Q242835.description: mythical musician and ruler at Thebes
Q242835.lead: Amphion and Zethus (Ancient Greek: Ζῆθος, romanized: Zêthos) were, in ancient Greek mythology, the twin sons of Zeus (or Theobus) by Antiope. They are important characters in one of the two founding myths of the city of Thebes, because they constructed the city's walls.

Q2430376.label: Thyone
Q2430376.description: Greek divinity or epithet for Semele mother of Dionysus

Q2436714.label: Tisiphone
Q2436714.description: daughter of Alcmaeon in Greek mythology
Q2436714.lead: In Greek mythology, Tisiphone is the daughter of Alcmaeon, Argive hero and one of the Epigoni, and Manto, the daughter of Tiresias. As an infant Tisiphone was given to the care of the royal couple of Corinth, but as she grew up the queen sold her as slave, envious of her great beauty.

Q2445677.label: Myrmidon
Q2445677.description: Greek mythical character, eponymous ancestor of the Myrmidons
Q2445677.lead: In Greek mythology, Myrmidon was the eponymous ancestor of the Myrmidons in one version of the myth.

Q2446711.label: Pamphylus
Q2446711.description: son of Aegimius in Greek mythology
Q2446711.lead: In Greek mythology, Pamphylus was a Dorian hero. He was considered to be the eponymous hero of one of the three tribes (phylai) of the Dorians, the Pamphyloi; his brothers, Dymas and Hyllos, were associated with the remaining two.

Q2446902.label: Ancaeus
Q2446902.description: son of Lykourgos, Greek mythological figure
Q2446902.lead: In Greek mythology, Ancaeus was both an Argonaut and a participant in the Calydonian Boar hunt, in which he met his end.

Q2463695.label: Pallas
Q2463695.description: son of Uranus and Gaia, killed and flayed by Athena
Q2463695.lead: In Greek mythology, Pallas was one of the Gigantes (Giants), the offspring of Gaia, born from the blood of the castrated Uranus. According to the mythographer Apollodorus, during the Gigantomachy, the cosmic battle of the Giants with the Olympian gods, he was flayed by Athena, who used his skin as a shield.

Q2470261.label: Miletus
Q2470261.lead: Miletus was a character from Greek mythology, the eponymous mythical founder of the city of Miletus.

Q247617.label: Curetes
Q247617.description: minor Minoan and Greek deities, servants of Rhea

Q250506.label: Tydeus
Q250506.description: son of Oeneus in Greek mythology
Q250506.lead: Tydeus was an Aetolian hero in Greek mythology, belonging to the generation before the Trojan War. He was one of the Seven against Thebes, and the father of Diomedes, who is frequently known by the patronymic Tydides.

Q252387.label: Palamedes
Q252387.lead: Palamedes was a Euboean prince, son of King Nauplius in Greek mythology. He joined the rest of the Greeks in the expedition against Troy.

Q2599183.label: Nyctimus
Q2599183.description: youngest or oldest of the 50 sons of Lycaon
Q2599183.lead: In Greek mythology, Nyctimus was an Arcadian prince and the youngest of the 50 sons of the impious King Lycaon either by the naiad Cyllene, Nonacris, or by an unknown woman.

Q2608087.label: Thasus
Q2608087.lead: In Greek mythology, Thasus or Thasos was a son of Poseidon (in other versions, Agenor, Phoenix or Cilix). He was a Phoenician prince and one of those who set out from Phoenicia in search of Europa (Thasus' sister).

Q2627407.label: Polyphemus
Q2627407.lead: In Greek mythology, Polyphemus was a Greek hero and also an Argonaut from Larissa.

Q2629041.label: Phylacus
Q2629041.description: mythical son of Deion, eponym of Phylace

Q26296.label: Electryon
Q26296.description: son of Perseus in Greek mythology
Q26296.lead: In Greek mythology, Electryon was a king of Tiryns and Mycenae or Medea in Argolis.

Q26399341.label: Cyrene
Q26399341.description: nymph, mother of Diomedes by Ares

Q2640491.label: Schoeneus
Q2640491.description: father of Atalante in Greek mythology

Q2641203.label: Copreus
Q2641203.description: King Eurystheus' herald in Greek mythology
Q2641203.lead: In Greek mythology, Copreus was King Eurystheus' herald who announced Heracles' Twelve Labours.

Q26690165.label: Anogon
Q26690165.description: Greek mythical character, son of Castor an Hilaeira
Q26690165.lead: In Greek mythology, Anogon was the son of Castor, one of the Dioscuri, and Hilaeira, daughter of Leucippus of Messenia. He was also called Anaxias.

Q269058.label: Glauce
Q269058.description: mythical character; daughter of Creon in Greek mythology
Q269058.lead: In Greek mythology, Creusa or Glauce (Γλαυκή "blue-gray"), Latin Glauca, was a princess of Corinth as the daughter of King Creon.

Q269243.label: Triptolemus
Q269243.description: mythical promulgator of agriculture at Eleusis
Q269243.lead: Triptolemus, also known as Buzyges (Ancient Greek: Βουζύγης, romanized: Bouzýgēs, lit. 'Bull-hitcher'), was a hero of Eleusis in Greek mythology, central to the Eleusinian Mysteries and is worshipped as the inventor and patron of agriculture. Triptolemus is credited with being the first to sow seed for cultivation after being taught by Demeter and is credited for the use of oxen and the plough.

Q270117.label: Lycurgus of Thrace
Q270117.description: mythological king of the Edoni in Thrace
Q270117.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycurgus was the king of the Edoni in Thrace, son of Dryas, the "oak", and father of a son whose name was also Dryas.

Q270867.label: Terra
Q270867.description: personification of the Earth in ancient Roman religion and mythology
Q270867.lead: In ancient Roman religion and mythology, Tellus, Terra, Tellus Mater or Terra Mater ("Earth" or "Mother Earth") is the personification of the Earth. Although Tellus and Terra are hardly distinguishable during the Imperial era, Tellus was the name of the original earth goddess in the religious practices of the Republic or earlier.

Q271949.label: Procrustes
Q271949.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q271949.lead: In Greek mythology, Procrustes, also known as Prokoptas, Damastes (Δαμαστής, "subduer") or Polypemon, was a rogue smith and bandit from Attica who attacked people by stretching them or cutting off their legs, so as to force them to fit the size of an iron bed. The word Procrustean is thus used by analogy to describe, for example, situations where an arbitrary standard is used to measure success, while completely disregarding obvious harm that results from the effort.

Q272000.label: Deianira
Q272000.description: wife of Heracles in Greek mythology
Q272000.lead: Deianira, Deïanira, or Deianeira, also known as Dejanira, is a Calydonian princess in Greek mythology whose name translates as "man-destroyer" or "destroyer of her husband". She was the wife of Heracles and, in late Classical accounts, his unwitting murderer, killing him with the poisoned Shirt of Nessus.

Q272006.label: Antaeus
Q272006.description: giant in Greek and Amazigh (Berber) mythology
Q272006.lead: Antaeus, known to the Berbers as Anti, was a figure in Berber and Greek mythology. He was famed for his defeat by Heracles as part of the Labours of Heracles.

Q272047.label: Endymion
Q272047.description: son of Aethlius in Greek mythology
Q272047.lead: In Greek mythology, Endymion was variously a handsome Aeolian shepherd, hunter, or king who was said to rule and live at Olympia in Elis. He was also venerated and said to reside on Mount Latmus in Caria, on the west coast of Asia Minor.

Q27613.label: Cadmus
Q27613.description: mythological founder of Thebes, son of Agenor
Q27613.lead: In Greek mythology, Cadmus was the legendary founder of Boeotian Thebes. He was, alongside Perseus and Bellerophon, the greatest hero and slayer of monsters before the days of Heracles.

Q27949366.label: Megapenthes
Q27949366.description: figure in Greek mythology, son of Proetus, king of Argos
Q27949366.lead: In Greek mythology, Megapenthes was a king of Argos.

Q279566.label: Deipyle
Q279566.description: daughter of Adrastus in Greek mythology

Q2803572.label: Tisamenus
Q2803572.lead: Tisamenus, in Greek mythology, was a son of Orestes and Hermione, daughter of Menelaus, or Erigone, daughter of Aegisthus who were first cousins twice over (their mothers were half-sisters and their fathers were brothers), so Tisamenus had only five great-grandparents, instead of the usual eight. Tisamenus succeeded his father to the thrones of Argos, Mycenae and Sparta.

Q28122362.label: Chloris
Q28122362.description: wife of Neleus and daughter of Amphion
Q28122362.lead: In Greek mythology, Chloris was a Minyan princess.

Q281670.label: Pero
Q281670.description: Greek mythical figure, daughter of Neleus
Q281670.lead: In Greek mythology, Pero was a princess of Pylos.

Q28362782.label: Lysippe
Q28362782.description: Greek mythological character; daughter of Proetus

Q28744949.label: Phrasius
Q28744949.description: Greek seer sacrificed by Busiris in Greek mythology

Q2934546.label: Calybe
Q2934546.lead: Calybe may refer to the two distinct characters from Greek mythology: Calybe, a nymph who was a wife of the Trojan king Laomedon and the mother of Bucolion. Calybe, one of the follower of Dionysus in the Indian War.

Q301219.label: Erechtheus
Q301219.lead: Erechtheus in Greek mythology was a king of Athens, the founder of the polis and, in his role as god, attached to Poseidon, as "Poseidon Erechtheus". The name Erichthonius is carried by a son of Erechtheus, but Plutarch conflated the two names in the myth of the begetting of Erechtheus.

Q3043322.label: Deliades
Q3043322.lead: In Greek mythology, Deliades or Heliades (Ἡλιάδην) was a son of Glaucus, the son of Sisyphus. He was unintentionally killed by his own brother Bellerophon.

Q305607.label: Abas
Q305607.lead: In Greek mythology, Abas was the twelfth king of Argos. He was the great-grandfather of Perseus, and the founder of the towns Abae and Argos Pelasgikon.

Q308055.label: Abderus
Q308055.description: son of Hermes in Greek mythology
Q308055.lead: In Greek mythology, Abderus or Abderos was a divine hero, reputed by some to be one of Heracles' lovers (eromenoi), and reputedly a son of Hermes by some accounts, and eponym of Abdera, Thrace.

Q3088918.label: Aegipan
Q3088918.description: son of Apollo in Greek mythology
Q3088918.lead: Aegipan was a mythological being, either distinct from or identical to Pan. His story appears to be of late origin.

Q311536.label: Aristomachus
Q311536.description: one of the Heracleidae, a great-grandson of Heracles

Q31256.label: Corinthos
Q31256.description: king of Corinth in Greek Mythology
Q31256.lead: In Greek mythology, Corinthus may refer to the following personages: Corinthus, the eponymous founder of the city of Corinth and the adjacent land. According to the local Corinthian tradition, he was a son of Zeus, but this tradition was not followed elsewhere.

Q3141720.label: Ocypete
Q3141720.description: one of the Harpies in Greek mythology
Q3141720.lead: Ocypete was one of the three Harpies in Greek mythology. She was also known as Ocypode (Ὠκυπόδη means "swift foot") or Ocythoe (Ὠκυθόη means "swift runner").

Q3147753.label: Ida
Q3147753.lead: In Greek mythology, Ida or Ide was one of the nurses of the infant Zeus on Crete.

Q31954.label: Polybus of Corinth
Q31954.lead: Polybus is a figure in Greek mythology. He was the king of Corinth whose wife was variously referred to as Periboea, Merope or Medusa, daughter of Orsilochus.

Q320449.label: Alcestis
Q320449.description: daughter of Pelias in Greek mythology
